direct_claims: This chart summarizes how many countries in each world region are not full democracies versus full democracies grouped by how long they have remained full democracies, all for 2025.
The regions listed are Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania, South America, and a world total.
The source context says the data come from the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy.
Europe has the largest number of long-standing full democracies among the regions shown, including 15 countries in the 61-90 years category and 11 in the 31-60 years category.
Oceania also stands out for having many long-duration full democracies relative to its small number of non-full democracies, with 9 countries aged 31-60 and 2 aged 61-90 versus 1 non-full democracy.

According to the provided domain story, full democracies are systems where citizens can choose the chief executive and legislature in multi-party, uncertain elections and where freedoms of expression, assembly, and association are protected.
Within the world total, the largest full-democracy age band is 31-60 years with 35 countries, followed by 61-90 years with 24.
Newly established or relatively young full democracies are less common globally, with 10 countries in the 1-18 years group and 8 in the 19-30 years group.

Because the domain story defines full democracy partly in terms of electoral choice and freedoms of expression, assembly, and association, these counts are also indirectly relevant to civil liberties and political participation.
The data are regional aggregates rather than country-by-country listings, so they show broad distribution patterns but not which individual countries fall into each category.
South America has no countries in the 19-30 or 61-90 full-democracy bands in this dataset.
Asia has no countries in the 1-18 band and only one country in the 61-90 band.
Africa has no countries in the 61-90 band.

Africa and Asia are dominated by countries classified as not full democracies in this dataset. — derived by comparing Africa 49 not full democracies vs 7 full democracies total, and Asia 45 vs 4.
In this chart, the age bands indicate how long countries have continuously remained full democracies. — derived from the category labels and the title about long-standing full democracies.
At the world level, there are 77 full democracies across all age bands combined and 122 countries that are not full democracies. — derived by summing 10+8+35+24 and comparing with 122.
Europe has 31 full democracies in total, more than any other region shown. — derived by summing Europe’s age-band values 2+3+11+15.
North America has 15 full democracies in total, Oceania 13, South America 6, Africa 7, and Asia 4. — derived by summing each region’s full-democracy age bands.
The regional totals imply that democratic durability is unevenly distributed across the world. — derived from comparing regional counts across age bands and non-full-democracy totals.

This data matters because it distinguishes between countries that currently meet a democratic standard and countries that have maintained that standard over long periods. — derived from the separation between non-full democracies and multiple longevity bands.
The world total shows that more countries are not full democracies than are full democracies, 122 versus 77. — derived by comparing world counts.

If policymakers, researchers, or advocates use this dataset, they can identify regions where full democracy is rare or relatively recent, such as Africa and Asia in this table. — derived from regional comparisons in the provided data.

If the current distribution persists, global democracy would remain geographically concentrated rather than evenly spread across regions. — derived from the 2025 regional distribution shown.
The world row matches the sum of the regional rows in every category shown. — derived by checking category sums across all regions.
